findings.headline: Workforce turnover improving overall but elevated in social care and hard-to-recruit professional areas
findings.detail: Annual turnover improved to 7.5% (12 months to June 2026) from 8.5% previously, indicating a stable overall position. However, social care and other hard-to-recruit areas show higher turnover rates. HR is building capacity for workforce planning and succession planning to manage these risks.
findings.matters: High turnover in social care directly increases recruitment, training and temporary staffing costs; it also affects service continuity and delivery quality in a major budget area.
findings.figures: 7.5% overall turnover vs 8.5% prior 12 months; higher rates in social care and professional areas
findings.quote: The Council's annual workforce turnover rate was 7.5% for the rolling 12 months to the end of June 2026. This is an improvement against 8.5% the previous 12 months, indicating a comparatively stable overall workforce position. Although turnover is not consistent across all services, with higher rates typically seen in social care and other hard-to-recruit professional areas.

findings.headline: Supported living capital pipeline shows 142 units in development with extended delivery timescale
findings.detail: To reduce reliance on residential care, the council has 142 units in the supported living pipeline: 16 expected by end 2026, 36 by end 2027, with further units beyond. The council is in regular contact with housing developers but notes an estimated 2-year delivery period.
findings.matters: The extended delivery timeline and scale of the pipeline indicate significant capital investment planned in adult social care housing; delays would extend the period of higher-cost residential placements.
findings.figures: 142 units in development; 16 expected end 2026; 36 expected end 2027; estimated 2-year delivery period; 34 people moved to supported living in Q1 (13 from residential)
findings.quote: In the current pipeline there are 142 units in development. 16 of these are expected to be completed by the end of 2026 and 36 are expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

findings.headline: Category 2 highway defect response fell to 73% from 81%, attributed to severe winter weather and network deterioration
findings.detail: Highway defect response performance is mixed: Category 1 improved to 94% from 84%, Category 3 improved to 92% from 89%, but Category 2 declined to 73% from 81% in Q1. The decline is attributed to severe winter weather and ongoing deterioration placing pressure on Via EM Ltd resources. The council plans continued capital investment and operational activity.
findings.matters: Deteriorating highway condition and rising maintenance costs indicate increasing capital spend pressure; Via EM Ltd pressure also signals outsourced service delivery strain.
findings.figures: Category 2: 73% vs 81% prior quarter; Category 1: 94% vs 84%; Category 3: 92% vs 89%; A roads: 98% not requiring maintenance; B/C roads: 96% not requiring maintenance
findings.quote: However, Category 2 repairs declined from 81% in Q4 to 73% in Q1, reflecting the impact of severe winter weather and ongoing deterioration within the highway network, which placed additional pressure on Via EM Ltd. resources.

findings.headline: 40,000 premises still lack adequate broadband following cancellation of Project Gigabit Lot 10
findings.detail: Despite 92.4% of premises achieving gigabit-capable broadband access by end of 2025/26, around 40,000 properties in rural areas remain unserved after the Government cancelled Project Gigabit Lot 10. The council is seeking replacement investment through Government, EMCCA and industry partners.
findings.matters: Digital infrastructure gaps affect economic development capacity, business location decisions, and the council's ability to deliver efficient digital services, all relevant to fiscal resilience.
findings.figures: 92.4% of premises gigabit-capable; ~40,000 premises unserved; Project Gigabit Lot 10 cancelled
findings.quote: Despite this progress, challenges remain for some rural communities following the cancellation of Project Gigabit Lot 10, with around 40,000 premises still awaiting broadband upgrades.

findings.headline: Access to social care information and advice remains below target at 64.6%, declining from 71.5% in 2022/23
findings.detail: Only 64.6% of adult social care service users find it easy to access information about support (2024/25 data), below the 71.8% target and 67.8% benchmark average. This represents a decline from 71.5% in 2022/23. The council launched Your Notts Directory in spring 2026 to consolidate information; it received 128,037 unique visitors in Q1 and contains 6,000 service listings from 3,000 organisations.
findings.matters: Poor information access can delay support-seeking, leading to crisis interventions and higher cost social care episodes; it also affects financial sustainability through preventive care outcomes.
findings.figures: 64.6% actual vs 71.8% target; benchmark 67.8%; declined from 71.5% in 2022/23; Your Notts Directory had 128,037 Q1 visitors
findings.quote: The latest available data (2024/25) shows that 64.6% of people using adult social care services found it easy to find information about services and support. This is below the local target of 71.8% and below the benchmark average of 67.8%, and performance has declined from 71.5% in 2022/23.

findings.headline: Carers' satisfaction with social contact dropped significantly to 18.8% against 33% target
findings.detail: The latest carers' survey (2025/26) shows satisfaction with social contact at 18.8%, well below both the local target of 33% and national benchmark of 30%. Overall satisfaction with social services also fell to 37.9% from previous levels. Both metrics have declined since the 2023/24 survey. The council is reviewing Short Breaks and developing wellbeing funding.
findings.matters: Lower carer satisfaction and wellbeing can affect the sustainability of informal care arrangements, leading to increased formal social care demand and cost pressures on the council.
findings.figures: 18.8% actual vs 33% target; 37.9% overall satisfaction vs 42.6% target; both declined from 2023/24
findings.quote: Satisfaction with the amount of social contact carers have was 18.8%, significantly below both the local target of 33% and the national benchmark of 30%. Both indicators have declined from the previous survey in 2023/24.

findings.headline: Family-based care placements significantly below target, with 13.4-point gap to 75%
findings.detail: Only 61.6% of looked after children are in family-based settings against the local target of 75%. The council acknowledges continued reliance on residential care and has identified over 180 improvement opportunities through the Valuing Care framework, plus a reunification pathway for 30 children. Wider market sufficiency challenges in fostering and placements are cited.
findings.matters: Residential care placements are significantly more costly than family-based settings; this gap directly drives higher spend and reduces financial sustainability in children's services.
findings.figures: 61.6% actual vs 75% target; 180 opportunities identified; 30 children in reunification pathway; 16- and 17-year-old reviews underway
findings.quote: At the end of Q1, 61.6% of looked after children were living in a family-based setting. This is below the local target of 75% by 13.4 percentage points.

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position Quarter 1 - 2026-27
findings.headline: Supreme Court judgment on 2 June 2026 fundamentally changed deprivation of liberty safeguards practice, with unknown cost implications.
findings.detail: A Supreme Court judgment on 2 June 2026 changed the legal definition of deprivation of liberty away from the Cheshire West test, requiring a broader multifactorial assessment instead. The council has updated guidance and trained staff, but further national guidance is pending. The department is monitoring referral numbers carefully during adjustment.
findings.matters: Regulatory changes to safeguarding practice drive workforce training costs and can alter caseload volumes and complexity if definition changes trigger new assessments.
findings.figures: Judgment effective 2 June 2026; DoLS median assessment time 20 days vs 31-day target; 87.7% of DoLS completed in 12 months
findings.quote: The Supreme Court judgment published on 2 June 2026 changed the definition of deprivation of liberty and confirmed that the previous Cheshire West 'acid test' should no longer be treated as the sole determining test.

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position Quarter 1 - 2026-27
findings.headline: Financial assessment waiting times have doubled, with 273 people waiting beyond the 28-day target.
findings.detail: Maximum wait time for financial assessment is now 97 days against a 28-day target, with median wait at 47 days. The council reports 273 people waiting beyond 28 days and a growing deputyship referral waiting list. These delays affect how quickly people receive clarity on financial contributions and support arrangements.
findings.matters: Service backlogs indicate operational inefficiency and constrain income collection; delays in assessment can also create risk of emergency spending when cases escalate.
findings.figures: Maximum wait 97 days vs 28-day target; median 47 days vs 28 days; 273 people beyond 28 days; 63 deputyship referrals on waiting list
findings.quote: There is also ongoing pressure within deputyship services, with a growing waiting list for referrals. These delays can affect how quickly people receive clarity about financial contributions and support arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position Quarter 1 - 2026-27
findings.headline: Adult Social Care forecasting breakeven position in Q1 2026-27, a significant improvement on recent deficit years.
findings.detail: At the end of the first quarter (June 2026), Adult Social Care is forecasting breakeven. This represents a significant improvement on recent financial years and is supported by verified savings in known pressure areas including Supported Accommodation.
findings.matters: Councils with chronic social care deficits carry higher financial risk; a shift to breakeven signals improved financial management and reduced pressure on reserves.
findings.figures: Breakeven forecast at period 3 2026-27; prior years in deficit
findings.quote: At the end of June 2026, the end of the first quarter, Adult Social Care is forecasting a breakeven position. This represents a significant improvement on recent financial years and is supported by evidence of changes in practice.

findings.paper_title: Audit - Internal Audit Term 3 Progress 2025-26 and Term 2 Plan 2026-27
findings.headline: School audits reveal persistent control weaknesses in separation of duties over payroll and payments
findings.detail: Schools are consistently receiving Limited Assurance opinions due to failures in separation of duties and authorization over overtime, payroll, payments and purchase orders. The report describes this as a recurring problem affecting schools regardless of office staffing levels, often linked to high turnover and lack of knowledge.
findings.matters: Recurring school control weaknesses increase fraud and error risk and indicate systemic control framework deficiencies affecting multiple budget holders within the council.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinions issued to schools in Term 3
findings.quote: The main reason for Limited Assurance on school audits is usually the issue of internal controls in relation to separation of duties and authorisation, over overtime, payroll, payments and purchase orders, etc. This problem arises at schools regardless of the number of office staff.

findings.paper_title: Audit - Internal Audit Term 3 Progress 2025-26 and Term 2 Plan 2026-27
findings.headline: Audit staffing shortages are causing planned assurance reviews to be deprioritized
findings.detail: The report states that the impact of staffing changes is reflected in audit completion rates, requiring agile approach to prioritize immediate council risks. This has resulted in some planned assurance reviews being deferred to later terms.
findings.matters: Reduced audit coverage means the council may not have full visibility of control weaknesses in key financial systems during the recovery period.
findings.figures: Audit days fell from 258 in 24/25 Term 2 to a low of 166 in 25/26 Term 3, with planned recovery to 220 in 26/27 Term 2
findings.quote: This can have an impact on delivery of the planned assurance reviews, but these are kept under review for ongoing priority in subsequent plans.

findings.paper_title: Audit - Internal Audit Term 3 Progress 2025-26 and Term 2 Plan 2026-27
findings.headline: Internal audit team lost 60% of senior auditor capacity through early retirements
findings.detail: The internal audit function has five senior auditor posts. Three were lost through early retirements. Replacement recruitment was underway with one starting in March 2026, another in June 2026, and recruitment ongoing for the third vacancy. This staffing reduction has required audit plans to be adjusted.
findings.matters: Reduced audit capacity limits the council's ability to independently verify financial and operational controls, which is critical assurance for lenders and the finance director.
findings.figures: 3 of 5 senior auditor posts lost through early retirements
findings.quote: The team has five senior auditor posts. Our staffing was reduced by three early retirements of senior auditors. Interviews have been arranged for replacements, one starting in March 2026, another in June 2026, and recruitment is currently in progress for the third vacancy.

findings.paper_title: Nottinghamshire Secondary School Place Sufficiency and Impact of Budget Pressure for School Places Programme
findings.headline: Council will incur additional home-to-school transport costs for approximately 338 pupils displaced outside their local planning areas.
findings.detail: The paper identifies transport cost as a direct consequence of project cancellation. It states 'A risk of the capital projects being cancelled is that this could result in the Council incurring increased home-to-school transport costs for pupils offered alternative places outside their local planning areas.' This represents an ongoing revenue pressure for multiple years, with pupils potentially placed far from home.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted transport costs are a recurring revenue pressure that will consume general fund resources and reduce financial flexibility, with no mechanism to reduce them if demand remains high.
findings.figures: 338 pupils requiring transport outside local area
findings.quote: A risk of the capital projects being cancelled is that this could result in the Council incurring increased home-to-school transport costs for pupils offered alternative places outside their local planning areas.

findings.paper_title: Nottinghamshire Secondary School Place Sufficiency and Impact of Budget Pressure for School Places Programme
findings.headline: Pausing projects will increase placement of pupils in higher-cost Independent Non-Maintained schools, putting pressure on the High Needs block.
findings.detail: The financial section warns that pausing these projects will force the council into more expensive provision. The paper identifies this as a direct consequence: 'Pausing the projects outlined in the report will likely result in more pupils being placed in higher costing Independent Non-Maintained schools, putting pressure on the High Needs block.' This shifts spending from one-time capital to ongoing revenue pressure.
findings.matters: High Needs block pressure is a known budget vulnerability for councils. Shifting from mainstream school expansion to specialist Independent Non-Maintained placements represents a permanent revenue commitment with inflationary cost growth.
findings.figures: Not specified; described as 'higher costing'
findings.quote: Pausing the projects outlined in the report will likely result in more pupils being placed in higher costing Independent Non-Maintained schools, putting pressure on the High Needs block.

findings.paper_title: Nottinghamshire Secondary School Place Sufficiency and Impact of Budget Pressure for School Places Programme
findings.headline: DfE has allocated significantly less Basic Need capital funding than expected, forcing pause of four school building projects totalling at least £6.3 million.
findings.detail: The Department for Education has drastically reduced capital allocation for school place expansion. The council is pausing: Serlby Park Academy (£2.8M, 50 additional places), Carlton Academy (£3.5M, 40 places for 2027-2028), South Nottinghamshire Academy (30 permanent places lost), and Lady Bay Primary School expansion. The paper states no further funding allocations are expected until spring 2027.
findings.matters: Unfunded capital projects indicate either the council's planning process is misaligned with central government intentions, or the council faces an ongoing structural funding gap that must be absorbed elsewhere.
findings.figures: £2.8M Serlby Park; £3.5M Carlton Academy; 50, 40, 30 additional places respectively; no further funding until spring 2027
findings.quote: This year the DFE has allocated Nottinghamshire with significantly less Basic Need Capital funding than expected and as a consequence, currently planned capital projects to boost secondary school capacity for 2027-2030 will not be completed within necessary time scales.

findings.paper_title: Nottinghamshire Secondary School Place Sufficiency and Impact of Budget Pressure for School Places Programme
findings.headline: Up to 28 year 7 pupils could be without a school place in September 2027, creating a statutory duty breach.
findings.detail: The council faces unprecedented pressure on secondary school places due to DfE underfunding. The paper explicitly identifies this as a breach risk: 'Approximately 28 year 7 Nottinghamshire pupils could be totally without a school place in September 2027 with similar shortages in the following two years.' In addition, 338 pupils will require transport outside their local area and 12 planning areas will have insufficiency of places in September 2027 and 2028.
findings.matters: Breaching statutory education duties represents a material governance failure that affects the council's creditworthiness and could trigger intervention from central government.
findings.figures: 28 pupils without a place September 2027; 338 pupils requiring transport outside local area; insufficiency in 12 planning areas
findings.quote: Approximately 28 year 7 Nottinghamshire pupils could be totally without a school place in September 2027 with similar shortages in the following two years. This would be a breach of the Council's statutory duty.

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Strategy and Land Development Programme 2025-29 - Gamston Development Site Funding - Final Tranche
findings.headline: Complex multi-party coordination required; failure to negotiate equalisation agreement could leave council financially disadvantaged
findings.detail: The site is owned or promoted by three parties: Nottinghamshire CC, Taylor Wimpey/Barwood, and Vistry Homes. Over £300m in public infrastructure is committed. If the equalisation agreement is not negotiated effectively, the council could be disadvantaged financially. The document notes risks around phasing, cost sharing, infrastructure delivery and timing if collaboration fails.
findings.matters: The capital receipt depends on a complex negotiation with other developers; loss of control over negotiations could reduce the proceeds the council receives
findings.figures: Over £300m in public infrastructure committed; over 4,000 dwellings planned
findings.quote: If an equalisation agreement is not negotiated effectively, the Council could be disadvantaged financially.

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Strategy and Land Development Programme 2025-29 - Gamston Development Site Funding - Final Tranche
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation may delay or prevent the capital receipt being realised by the current council
findings.detail: The government has indicated its intention to progress LGR resulting in new unitary authorities with vesting day in 2028. The council may receive the capital receipt before vesting day, but this cannot be guaranteed and depends on disposal timing. If disposal occurs later, the receipt accrues to the successor authority, not Nottinghamshire CC.
findings.matters: For a lender, the uncertainty about which entity will hold the asset and receipt matters for both security and repayment; the council may lose control of the asset and proceeds within the planning window
findings.figures: Anticipated vesting day 2028; disposal expected 2027–28
findings.quote: Due to the anticipated timings, the current programme indicates that it may be possible for the Council to receive a proportion of the capital receipt prior to the anticipated vesting day of the new unitary authorities in 2028, this cannot be guaranteed and will be dependent upon the timing of the disposal and the agreed payment structure.

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Strategy and Land Development Programme 2025-29 - Gamston Development Site Funding - Final Tranche
findings.headline: Project costs have already overrun by £548k (31% above original allocation) due to transition from indicative to fully costed estimates
findings.detail: The council was allocated £1.765m by the Corporate Asset Management Group in June 2026. This final tranche request of £1.938m exceeds that by £548k. The increase reflects transition from initial estimates to fully developed costings and inclusion of agency and disposal fees not previously accounted for.
findings.matters: Early cost escalation signals risk of further overruns; the council is already borrowing more than originally planned to bring the site to market
findings.figures: Original allocation £1,764,865; total now requested £2,312,865; increase £548,000
findings.quote: This exceeds the original allocation of £1,764,865 approved by the Capital & Asset Management Group on the 4th June 2026 by £548,000. This increase reflects the transition from initial indicative cost estimates to fully developed costings, together with the inclusion of agency and disposal fees that were not previously accounted for.

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Strategy and Land Development Programme 2025-29 - Gamston Development Site Funding - Final Tranche
findings.headline: Council borrowing £1.2m ahead of receiving disposal proceeds for a major land sale
findings.detail: The council is funding £2.3m in total pre-disposal costs through capital borrowing (£1.22m) and future capital receipts (£718k via CIPFA 4% cap). The financial implication is that these costs will be incurred before the council receives any capital receipt from the disposal. Disposal is not expected until 2027–28 at earliest.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the timing mismatch between capital expenditure and receipt, and the risks if the planned capital receipt does not materialize
findings.figures: £1,219,787 capital programme increase; £718,078 to be funded from capital receipt; total project cost £2,312,865
findings.quote: The financial implication for the Council is that these costs will be incurred and funded in advance of receiving a capital receipt from the disposal of the site.

findings.headline: National Living Wage increases create £30m unavoidable cost pressure across three-year MTFS
findings.detail: The National Living Wage is rising to £12.71 in April 2026 with further 4.42% annual increases forecast. External care provider costs from NLW increases alone total £9.52m in 2026/27, £9.94m in 2027/28, and £10.55m in 2028/29. These cost increases flow directly through to provider contracts and cannot be absorbed locally or avoided through service redesign.
findings.matters: Social care provision in England is heavily dependent on private and voluntary sector providers, particularly for external placements. NLW inflation is an economy-wide shock that affects all councils equally and cannot be managed through local efficiency savings. It represents a structural erosion of budget purchasing power.
findings.figures: £30.014m NLW external provider cost pressure across MTFS; £12.71 minimum wage April 2026; 4.42% annual inflation assumed
findings.quote: The National Living wage is increased each year, the current rate is £12.21. Rates used for 26/27 £12.71 (Actual), 4.42% inflation for 26/27 = £13.27 and 4.42% inflation for 28/29 = £13.86.

findings.headline: Current year 2025/26 forecast overspend of £5.9m will be funded from General Fund reserves, which stood at £35.9m
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £5.9m overspend in 2025/26, comprised of £11.1m net portfolio overspend mainly in Adult Social Care, offset by underspends in central items. This shortfall will be managed through reserve drawdown. At 31 March 2025, the General Fund balance was £35.9m. The MTFS also embeds use of £27.9m of earmarked reserves across the three-year period.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite buffer, not a sustainable funding source. The council is using reserves to manage current-year pressures rather than bringing recurring expenditure into line with recurring income. Combined with planned reserve usage across the MTFS, this creates a trajectory of reserve depletion that reduces financial flexibility, increases borrowing risk, and limits headroom for unexpected shocks.
findings.figures: £5.9m forecast overspend 2025/26; General Fund balance 31 March 2025 £35.9m; £27.9m planned reserve usage across MTFS
findings.quote: the Council reported a forecast overspend of £5.9m in the current financial year. This out-turn is comprised of a net £11.1m portfolio overspend mainly because of forecast overspends in Adult Social Care services.

findings.headline: £44.2m mitigation programme is essential to prevent deficits, with non-achievement identified as common cause of in-year overspends
findings.detail: The MTFS shows £40.0m of gross budget pressures being mitigated to a net reduction of £4.2m through £44.2m of planned savings and interventions across the three-year period. The report explicitly flags that non-achievement of savings and mitigation plans is one of two most prevalent reasons for in-year overspends across the English local government sector (the other being demand increases). A contingency analysis shows a 30% delivery failure would create a £13.3m additional deficit.
findings.matters: A balanced budget that depends on delivery of a large transformation programme creates execution risk. If the council fails to achieve planned mitigations, a forecast balanced budget becomes a deficit requiring either additional reserves drawdown, borrowing, or emergency cuts. This transforms budget sustainability from an achievement problem into a delivery problem.
findings.figures: £44.2m total mitigations required; £40.0m gross pressures; 30% contingency impact £13.3m additional deficit; 20% contingency £8.8m
findings.quote: the net level of pressures is heavily reliant on full achievement of a £44.2m mitigation programme. It should be noted that the most prevalent reasons for in-year overspends across the local government sector are (i) increases in demand and (ii) non-achievement of savings / mitigation plans.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand pressures increased £4.5m in 2026-27 with care package costs of £14.059m, driven by complexity and demographic change
findings.detail: The MTFS shows care package demand for adults aged 18-64 of £14.059m in 2026/27 alone, with £24.935m across the full three-year MTFS period. This reflects both volume growth and higher cost per individual due to advances in childhood healthcare meaning more individuals with complex physical and learning disabilities are living into adulthood. The paper notes these are 'particular headwinds' including increased complex needs, provider cost pressures, and requests from ICB partners to share in their fiscal challenges.
findings.matters: Social care is the largest controllable spend for councils and this is a structural, demographic demand that cannot be managed through efficiency savings alone. Statutory duties require funding of assessed care packages. If demand growth continues to exceed funding growth, the council faces either further service restriction or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £14.059m care package demand 2026/27; £24.935m across MTFS; £4.5m increase in adult social care portfolio 2026/27 due to care package demand
findings.quote: Care Package Demand for Adults Aged 18-64 Years 14,059 [2026/27]... This budget pressure reflects rising demand and increasing complexity in care for working-age adults (under 65), including young adults transitioning from children's services. Advances in childhood healthcare mean more individuals with complex physical and learning disabilities are living into adulthood.

findings.headline: Pensions administration staffing concerns: committee requested a deep dive into resourcing of the pensions administration team, deferred pending new manager review
findings.detail: The committee requested on 12 February 2026 a deep dive into the resourcing of the pensions administration team. This review has been deferred to later in the year pending a new Pensions Administration Manager reviewing available resourcing before making recommendations. This signals staffing or capacity concerns that warrant investigation.
findings.matters: Under-resourcing of pension fund administration could lead to service failures, regulatory breaches, or member disputes that impose costs or liability on the council.
findings.figures: One new Pensions Administration Manager appointed; deep dive deferred to later in 2026
findings.quote: At its meeting on 12 February 2026, the committee asked for a deep dive into the resourcing of the pensions administration team. Given the extent of this work and the recent appointment of a new Pensions Administration Manager, this deep dive will be presented later in the year.

findings.headline: Data governance resourcing: committee approved a Data Improvement Plan and funding for two additional data officers on 30 April 2026
findings.detail: The risk register updates show that on 30 April 2026 the committee approved a Data Improvement Plan and provided funding for two data officers to undertake the next stage of mortality screening and address verification. This indicates recent investment in addressing data quality and governance within the pension fund.
findings.matters: A pension fund with data quality issues could create administrative failures in member records or payment systems, which could expose the council to regulatory action or member disputes that affect council finances.
findings.figures: Two data officers funded; decision dated 30 April 2026
findings.quote: Adm 1 – update to existing controls and planned controls to reflect the decision made by committee on 30 April 2026 to approve the Data Improvement Plan and to move to the next stage of mortality screening and data improving. Planned controls have also been updated to reflect these decisions, together with the decision to approve funding for two data officers

findings.headline: Dissolution of Business Rates pooling removes income stabilisation that operated for 13 years
findings.detail: The Nottinghamshire Business Rates pool, which the council notes provided 'significant benefits' since 2013/14, is being dissolved at the end of 2025/26. The council will review 2026/27 business rates income to determine if pooling is viable in 2027/28, but this is uncertain and the council may face greater income volatility.
findings.matters: Business rates income is volatile. Loss of pooling makes the council more exposed to economic downturns affecting its commercial base.
findings.figures: Business Rates pool operated since 2013/14, dissolution effective end of 2025/26
findings.quote: Note the significant benefits of operating the Nottinghamshire Business Rates pool since 2013/14, the dissolution of the Nottinghamshire Business Rates pool at the end of 2025/26

findings.headline: New borrowing cycle initiated with £70m in 2026/27, rising to £120m cumulative by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council is borrowing for the first time in three years, with £70m borrowed in 2026/27 and a further £50m in 2027/28. This represents a £120m increase in external debt over two years. The borrowing requirement previously showed no borrowing needed to 2025/26.
findings.matters: Debt levels are increasing materially just as reserves are declining, reducing overall financial flexibility. Lenders need to understand what capital schemes drive this borrowing and the returns on that investment.
findings.figures: Annual borrowing 2026/27 £70m, 2027/28 £50m, cumulative £120m
findings.quote: Annual borrowing requirement (nearest £10m) 0.0 0.0 70.0 50.0 0.0 ... Cumulative annual borrowing requirement 0.0 0.0 70.0 120.0 120.0

findings.headline: Reserves declining significantly to £104.9m by end of 2027/28 before recovering
findings.detail: Usable reserves are forecast to decline from £206.6m at end of 2025/26 to £104.9m at end of 2027/28, a drop of nearly 50%. Whilst reserves recover to £165m by 2028/29, the intermediate drawdown shows the council is heavily dependent on reserve depletion to balance its budget during this period.
findings.matters: Rapidly declining reserves limit the council's ability to absorb service pressures or funding shortfalls. The £104.9m represents a materially lower cushion against the £880m budget.
findings.quote: Closing Capital Financing Requirement ... comprising: - Usable reserves 276.0 206.6 156.6 104.9 165.0

findings.headline: Potential unfunded liability for 10% of DSG High Needs deficits even after government support
findings.detail: The government is providing 90% support for DSG High Needs deficits accrued to end of 2025/26, but the council may still be liable for the remaining 10%. The council acknowledges this liability could be £17.8m to March 2028 or more, and that support is contingent on submitting and securing DfE approval of a SEND reform plan. Future support for deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28 has not yet been announced.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has adequate reserves to cover this potential liability, and how dependent the budget is on government announcements that may not materialise.
findings.figures: £17.8m to 31 March 2028, or more if future support is less than assumed; 90% government support for accumulated deficits
findings.quote: The treatment of the remaining 10% unfunded element is not clear and, potentially, the Council will still be liable for the 10% unfunded element (£17.8m to 31 March 2028, or more if future support is less than assumed.)

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position – Quarter 3 (October to December) 2025/2026
findings.headline: The Sustainability Plan mitigations cover less than half of identified budget pressures, suggesting the overspend risk will persist.
findings.detail: The department has identified total pressures of £18.70m but is only delivering mitigations of £8.76m (46.8% coverage). This gap of £9.94m is significantly larger than can be addressed by the £5m Central Finance contribution, indicating the department does not have identified solutions to close the overspend. The mitigations have remained static from Period 8 to Period 9 despite the overspend worsening.
findings.matters: When identified mitigations cover less than half of known pressures, it indicates a fundamental shortfall in the council's cost-control strategy. The persistence of this gap from P8 to P9, despite month-on-month overspend increases, suggests the Sustainability Plan is not being delivered at sufficient pace or scale.
findings.figures: £18.70m total identified pressures; £8.76m mitigations (46.8% of pressures); £9.94m unmitigated gap
findings.quote: At Period 9, ASCH are reporting an additional effect of (£8.76m) in the year from its Sustainability Plan in mitigation of estimated total pressures of £18.70m. This remains the same from period 8

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position – Quarter 3 (October to December) 2025/2026
findings.headline: Workforce sickness and agency staffing remain elevated, with high absence driven by stress, depression and anxiety creating operational and cost pressures.
findings.detail: The department reports 'high levels of sickness absence driven primarily by stress, depression and anxiety' with absence levels 'above corporate benchmarks'. Agency usage 'remained high in several areas' as recruitment stabilises. Staffing pressures are acute in Appointee and Deputyship teams and across Community Social Work and Therapy. Brokerage and financial assessment teams face particular strain, causing delays in Direct Payment setup and hindering the delivery of the Sustainability Plan.
findings.matters: Agency staff typically cost 30-40% more than permanent staff. Persistent high absence and agency usage indicate organisational stress and underlying workforce retention issues that will inflate staffing budgets. These teams (brokerage, financial assessment) are critical to the council's cost-control mechanisms.
findings.figures: No specific absence percentage given; agency usage remains high in several areas; staffing delays affecting DP setup
findings.quote: Internal workforce challenges continued during Quarter 3, with high levels of sickness absence driven primarily by stress, depression and anxiety. Vacancy rates varied across teams but showed modest improvements compared to earlier in the year as recruitment initiatives progressed and new starters joined neighbourhood teams. Absence levels remained above corporate benchmarks.

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position – Quarter 3 (October to December) 2025/2026
findings.headline: Only 63.8% of service users have received an annual review, against a 100% target, leaving approximately 1,397 people without current assessment of their needs.
findings.detail: Review completion is rated Red across all age groups (63.8% for all ages; 66.1% for 18-64; 61.8% for 65+). While the backlog has been reduced from over 2,100 to approximately 1,397, this remains a significant gap. Reviews are the mechanism through which social workers identify opportunities to step people down to more independent or lower-cost support arrangements. The report notes 'time lag between review activity and confirmed financial benefits (due to the 56 day verification period)', indicating reviews are critical to unlocking cost avoidance in the Sustainability Plan.
findings.matters: Without timely reviews, councils cannot identify and implement cost-saving opportunities. A backlog of this size represents both a governance weakness (failure to assess changing need) and a cost control failure, as higher-cost placements persist longer than necessary.
findings.figures: 63.8% reviewed (target 100%); 1,397 people in backlog (down from 2,100+); 56-day verification lag on financial benefits
findings.quote: Percentage of people in receipt of service for 12mths who have been reviewed in the last 12 months all age 63.8%

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position – Quarter 3 (October to December) 2025/2026
findings.headline: Older adults in residential and nursing care are 213 places above target, with demand continuing to rise.
findings.detail: The council is supporting 2,348 older adults (aged 65+) in long-term residential or nursing placements against a target of 2,135, representing a 9.9% overage. New admissions to older adult care (686) are consistently above quarterly targets. The report cites 'sustained upstream pressure from hospital pathways and deterioration in the community' as drivers, with intensive community support arrangements not being arranged quickly enough to prevent residential admission.
findings.matters: Residential care is the most expensive service type. Demand above target drives direct cost overspend. Sustained admission pressure indicates underlying service system issues (hospital discharge pathways, community capacity) that will be difficult to reverse quickly.
findings.figures: 2,348 actual vs 2,135 target (213 over, 9.9% variance); December new admissions: 686 (quarterly trend: 605, 656, 686)
findings.quote: For older adults (65+), the demand picture remained more challenging. New admissions showed a steady increase across the quarter, indicating sustained upstream pressure from hospital pathways and deterioration in the community —factors that often result in residential admission where intensive support cannot be arranged quickly enough at home.

findings.paper_title: Adult Social Care Performance, Risks and Financial Position – Quarter 3 (October to December) 2025/2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care forecast overspend has increased to £11.35m by Period 9, worsening from £9.94m at Period 8.
findings.detail: The department reported a forecast overspend of £11.35m (3.41% of the £327.19m budget) before the use of reserves. This represents a deterioration of £1.21m compared to Period 8. The Sustainability Plan is mitigating only £8.76m of identified pressures of £18.70m, and the council is receiving a £5m contribution from Central Finance to help manage the overspend.
findings.matters: A growing monthly overspend in the largest council service budget suggests deteriorating financial control and underlying demand or cost pressures that mitigations are not addressing. This pattern is a leading indicator of wider council financial distress.
findings.figures: £11.35m overspend (3.41% of budget); £1.21m increase from Period 8; £8.76m mitigations against £18.70m pressures; £5m Central Finance contribution
findings.quote: At Period 9 and after the impact of its Sustainability Plan, ASCH are reporting a forecast of £344.16m before the use of reserves, which is a forecast overspend for the year of £11.35m. This represents 3.41% of the departmental budget of £327.19m and is an increase of £1.21m on the £9.94m overspend reported at Period 8.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges significant uncertainty and medium-term financial challenges
findings.detail: The report states that due to the adverse variance and significant uncertainty and financial challenges facing the council over the medium term, there is a need to continually reinforce the message about budget management and in-year savings delivery.
findings.matters: The acknowledgement of medium-term financial challenges suggests this year's overspend is not a one-off problem; lenders would see this as signalling structural budget stress beyond 2026-27.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: due to this adverse variance and the significant levels of uncertainty and financial challenges facing the Council over the medium term, the key message to effectively manage budgets and, wherever possible, deliver in-year savings is being continually reinforced

findings.headline: Planning appeal requiring £0.5m contingency drawdown
findings.detail: An appeal on a planning decision is anticipated to create additional costs of £0.5m to be met by requesting contingency reserves. Combined with increased property maintenance costs of £0.6m in Economic Development and Asset Management, the portfolio faces £1.1m overspend.
findings.matters: Using contingency reserves for unplanned litigation and maintenance reduces financial flexibility to respond to emergencies or other unforeseen costs later in the year.
findings.figures: £0.5m planning appeal costs; £0.6m property maintenance overspend
findings.quote: with an appeal on a planning decision is anticipated to lead to additional costs of £0.5m which will be met by a request to use contingency

findings.headline: Increased demand for statutory SEND services creating £0.7m overspend
findings.detail: The Special Educational Needs and Disabilities service is forecasting a £0.7m overspend due to demand increase. This represents a second statutory demand-led budget area showing pressure alongside children's services.
findings.matters: SEND is a statutory service that cannot be rationed; demand-driven overages suggest growing need in the county and ongoing budget sustainability pressure in a protected service.
findings.figures: £0.7m overspend
findings.quote: An increase in demand for our statutory SEND service has resulted in a forecast overspend of £0.7m.

findings.headline: Unplanned surge in external children's home placements driving £3.7m overspend
findings.detail: The largest component of the overall overspend is an unplanned increase in the number of children placed in external children's homes, creating a £3.7m cost pressure. This occurs despite planned mitigations of £5.8m, and the report sets out several management actions to reduce the forecast.
findings.matters: Statutory children's services demand is unpredictable and cannot be refused; this shows the council's capacity planning is under strain and it faces recurring cost exposure in a high-pressure service area.
findings.figures: £3.7m overspend; £5.8m planned mitigations
findings.quote: there has been a significant increase in the number of children placed in external children's homes leading to an overspend of £3.7m

news_drafts.lead: High turnover in social care directly increases recruitment, training and temporary staffing costs; it also affects service continuity and delivery quality in a major budget area.

news_drafts.lead: The extended delivery timeline and scale of the pipeline indicate significant capital investment planned in adult social care housing; delays would extend the period of higher-cost residential placements.
